Methodology beyond the tier name is not given in the text.

Hardware context cited: ~$2k bimanual arm setups, 7 semi-humanoids under $15k, and Hugging Face's $399 Microduck selling 10,000+ units within days. Dream-1 is limited to bimanual parallel-gripper manipulation; mobile manipulators and dexterous hands are stated as future, not shipped.
summary: Dream Labs came out of stealth with $90M in seed funding and released Dream-1, a World Action Model served through a public API that the company says can control bimanual, parallel-gripper robots it never saw in training, including the 18-year-old PR2, with no per-robot fine-tuning or demonstrations. The approach predicts video and actions together and commands robots through a shared end-effector pose space, relying on head and wrist cameras so that unfamiliar grippers appear only as pixels; the robot's own inverse-kinematics solver turns predicted poses into joint commands, and the company notes zero-shot quality varies with that solver and across tasks. Dream Labs frames this as a way out of robotics' cold-start problem, pairing it with a hardware trend toward cheap bimanual arms and semi-humanoids. Self-reported running cost is $3/hr for Dream-1 and $2/hr for the lighter Dream-1-flash, roughly $0.0009-$0.0013 per action; when zero-shot is insufficient, a Fine-tuning-as-a-Service path adapts the model from minutes-to-hours of robot data and lifted language-following on 10 of 12 beta robots. Benchmark claims placing Dream-1 ahead of Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon at 16x lower cost come from Robocurve, described as an independent Public Benefit Corporation, but the post gives little methodology detail. The post is a vendor launch and states real limits: coverage is confined to bimanual parallel-gripper manipulation, and a gap between one-shot and zero-shot performance remains.
novelty: zero-shot control of unseen robot embodiments via World Action Models
audience: robotics/ML engineers tracking generalist robot policies

title: Everyone is doing Git on S3 wrong
why: If agents push every commit instead of batching, the single-repo write ceiling becomes the bottleneck, and Enroute's vendor benchmark claims 7,600 pushes/sec into one repo versus the ~120-300/sec Cursor reports for the S3-WAL design.
notes: The target is the S3-backed write-ahead-log design (Cursor/SpaceX 'Continuity', August, plus open-source clones like walgit): any machine rebuilds a repo from an immutable packfile log whose entries become visible via conditional PUTs to a single WAL index object. Reads scale (Cursor claims linear to 100 replicas), but writes serialize through that one index and must land on one on-disk copy, which Cursor reports caps at ~120 pushes/sec on S3 Standard and >300 on S3 Express One Zone.

Root problem with treating Git as plain content-addressed storage on S3: Git traverses a graph (ref to commit to tree to blobs, plus delta chains) where each next key is known only after the prior read returns, so each hop is a 30-40ms round trip. The fix both designs use is data locality via packfiles; Enroute's claim is it keeps locality without pinning a full on-disk copy per replica.

Enroute architecture: stateless compute tier plus a 'ledger' tier running one replicated log per repo with CockroachDB-style MultiRaft consensus holding refs and the layer list. Pushes build immutable 'layers' lock-free in parallel; only the ref commit is ordered via compare-and-swap. Small pushes inline into the log; layers >1 MiB go straight to the bucket. Appending a log entry is cited at 1-2ms with group-commit fsyncs, versus a bucket round trip.

Storage format cuts the object graph along commit boundaries into per-commit 'segments' grouped into immutable 'layers' (LSM-like: ~once/sec flush, merge ~8 similar layers into one ~8x larger, byte copies without recompression). Serving a fetch replays segments along common ancestry rather than walking the live graph. Caveats stated: duplicate objects across segments (deduped at build), shallow clones must send boundary deltas in full, partial clones rely on same-kind object clustering.

Benchmarks are self-reported. Peak 7,600 pushes/sec on a single repo (EC2+S3, forgemark); the author frames this as ~18x Entire.io and ~1,000x GitHub while explicitly noting the numbers come from different setups and give only order-of-magnitude. Versus stock Git 2.56.0 over git http-backend/Apache on linux.git: shallow clones >2x faster, partial clones on par, full clones ~17% slower, incremental fetches ~13% slower, with the lag blamed on more expensive client-side delta decoding. Cold vs warm full clone of linux.git: 128.6s vs 126.0s.

Listed gaps: no garbage collection yet (immutable layers leave unreachable objects after force-push/branch delete), HTTP smart protocol only (no SSH), no cross-node routing so repos cache redundantly, slow cold-start fetch performance, no compute autoscaling, and a planned server-side gRPC write API for agents.
summary: The post from Enroute argues that current S3-backed Git hosting designs, led by Cursor/SpaceX's August 'Continuity' work and its open-source imitators, scale reads well but serialize writes through a single write-ahead-log index per repository and still require every replica to hold a full on-disk copy of the repo. Enroute's alternative separates stateless compute from a storage tier whose 'ledger' runs one MultiRaft-replicated log per repo (holding refs and a layer list), with object storage for durability; pushes build immutable layers lock-free and only ref commits are ordered via compare-and-swap. A custom format cuts the object graph into per-commit segments grouped into immutable layers, letting the server answer clones/fetches by replaying segments along common ancestry instead of walking the graph, with LSM-style flush and compaction to the bucket. Self-reported benchmarks claim over 7,600 pushes/sec into one repository (framed loosely as ~18x Entire.io and ~1,000x GitHub, with the author noting differing setups), shallow clones over 2x faster than stock Git, but full clones ~17% and incremental fetches ~13% slower due to costlier client-side delta decoding. All performance numbers are vendor-produced, and the project still lacks garbage collection, SSH support, cross-node routing, and autoscaling.
novelty: critiques S3-backed Git WAL designs, proposes locality-first alternative
audience: infra engineers building or evaluating Git hosting at scale

title: OpenSSH 10.6
why: If you run sshd on Linux built with PAM disabled, 10.6p2 closes a password-authentication bypass; separately, OpenSSH has switched to shipping fixes in more frequent releases rather than batching them, so patch cadence just changed.
notes: 10.6p2 (2026-11-05): fixes a password authentication bypass exploitable via sshd(8) on Linux systems built and run with PAM support disabled (noted as affecting musl libc setups); the team says the root cause is outside sshd but is avoidable there. Reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield.

Release-policy change: OpenSSH reports that AI-identified security bugs are repeatedly rediscovered independently by other researchers, which it reads as evidence adversaries can find them too; for now it is making more frequent releases instead of batching fixes until the next planned one. Several fixes credit work 'in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research.'

10.6 Security: disables the LZ77 dictionary coder to mitigate the 'Crossing the Streams' chosen-plaintext side channel (Bäumer/Brinkmann, arXiv:2609.07709) that recovers secrets across multiplexed channels sharing one compression dictionary; compression is now less effective, and app-level compression is recommended instead. Also disallows '$' and '\\' in command-line usernames to block shell injection via ProxyCommand/Match exec.

Post-quantum: enables the hybrid ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 signature algorithm (dropping the prior experimental '@openssh.com' suffix, so old keys must be regenerated) and, in 10.6p2, allows it as a CA signature algorithm. WarnWeakCrypto is now on by default server-side and logs non-PQ-safe key agreement.

Deprecations: scp(1) -R (remote-to-remote copy) now emits a warning and will later be ignored, citing shell-quoting injection risk; support for platforms needing root for PTY allocation without fd-passing (QNX 6, SCO OpenServer 5) is slated for removal, and GatewayPorts/StreamLocalForwarding are forcibly disabled there now. The --disable-fd-passing configure option was removed.

Other 10.6 items: FIDO resident keys preserve credProtect PIN/biometric policy; ssh-add -P skips PIN where not required; new PubkeyAuthOptions max-pk-ok (default 6) separates key-probe tests from MaxAuthTries; default KDF rounds raised 24 to 32 with a 1M-round cap; fallback ed25519 switched from SUPERCOP to libsodium.
summary: OpenSSH 10.6 (2026-10-06) and the follow-up 10.6p2 (2026-11-05) ship security fixes alongside a stated change in release practice: because AI-found bugs are being independently rediscovered by other researchers, the team now releases bugfixes more frequently rather than batching them. 10.6p2's headline fix is a password-authentication bypass exploitable through sshd on Linux built with PAM disabled (musl setups), with the root cause described as outside sshd. 10.6 disables the LZ77 dictionary coder to mitigate the 'Crossing the Streams' compression side channel (arXiv:2609.07709), tightens command-line username parsing against shell injection, and enables the hybrid post-quantum signature ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 (requiring regeneration of experimentally-generated keys). It begins deprecating scp -R and support for platforms that need root for PTY allocation without fd-passing (QNX 6, SCO OpenServer 5), forcibly disabling GatewayPorts and StreamLocalForwarding on those platforms now. Several fixes credit collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research. All vendor and reporter claims here are self-reported in the release notes; no independent verification is provided.
novelty: AI-found bug reports now shaping OpenSSH release cadence
audience: sysadmins and security engineers maintaining SSH infrastructure

title: Hackers behind $6.3bn Binance heist ‘used malware and bogus job interviews’
why: The intrusion that drained $6.3bn from Binance started with a wallet engineer's laptop, not a smart-contract bug, so your supply-chain and social-engineering defenses matter more than your on-chain security.
notes: Binance's own post-incident update puts the total drained from hot wallets at $6.34bn, with $2.85bn frozen or intercepted; the rest remains unrecovered.
The chain started in June: a company engineer inadvertently downloaded malware that exposed the roles of the team maintaining Binance's cryptowallet infrastructure, mapping targets for later.

September phase used a recruitment lure: a fake project director contacted a second engineer on a job-hunting platform, ran a sham HR video interview and a 'CEO' chat-app interview, and used the second interview to plant malware.

Binance says that on Oct 20 the attacker combined the compromised machine with an internal AI tool to seize control of two wallet developers' systems; on Oct 29, using stolen credentials from the first engineer, they ran a malicious script from the second developer's computer to launch the theft. The article does not describe what the AI tool is or how it was abused.

FBI attributed the hack to North Korea; Kim Yo-jong called the claim 'absurd rhetoric' via KCNA. The article notes DPRK deepfake-interview tactics usually run the other way, with fake IT applicants seeking jobs to funnel money to Pyongyang.
Details of the attack chain are self-reported by Binance; no independent forensic confirmation is provided in the article.
summary: Binance disclosed the attack chain behind a $6.34bn hot-wallet theft, saying it began in June when an engineer inadvertently downloaded malware that exposed the wallet-infrastructure team's roles. In September, attackers ran a recruitment scam against a different engineer, using a fake job listing, a sham HR video interview, and a chat-app interview with a fictitious company's 'CEO' to deliver a second malware payload. On Oct 20 the attacker used the compromised machine plus an internal AI tool to take over two wallet developers' systems, and on Oct 29 used stolen credentials and a malicious script to trigger the theft; Binance says $2.85bn has been frozen or intercepted. The FBI blames North Korea, which denied involvement through Kim Yo-jong, calling the accusation 'absurd rhetoric.' The account is Binance's self-reported version, and the article gives no detail on the internal AI tool's nature or role.

title: Python 3.15.0 (final) is here!
why: If you ship Python, 3.15 flips two defaults that change your runtime: macOS binaries now install free-threading support out of the box, and Windows 64-bit binaries use the tail-calling interpreter, while explicit lazy imports (PEP 810) let you cut startup time without restructuring code.
notes: Scope: 5,643 commits from 1,012 contributors versus 3.14. Release team is Hugo van Kemenade, Ned Deily, and Steve Dower; van Kemenade's release-manager work was funded via the Sovereign Tech Fellowship.

JIT remains experimental; self-reported geometric-mean gains are 7-8% on x86-64 Linux over the standard interpreter and 11-12% on AArch64 macOS over the tail-calling interpreter. No benchmark suite or methodology is cited in the post.
New builtins and language features: PEP 661 sentinel type, PEP 814 frozendict type, PEP 810 explicit lazy imports, PEP 686 UTF-8 as the default encoding, PEP 798 unpacking in comprehensions.

Default shifts: macOS binaries install free-threading support by default; Windows 64-bit binaries switch to the tail-calling interpreter; PEP 831 enables frame pointers by default for system-level observability. Free-threaded stable ABI lands via PEP 803/820/793.

Known breakage: on macOS 27.0, tkinter/IDLE dialogs (About IDLE, Settings, Open Module) hang, requiring Force Quit. Cause is a macOS 27.0 behavior change affecting all current Tk versions; tracked in issue #158053, with deferring the OS upgrade suggested as a workaround.

Standard library and typing: PEP 799 adds a dedicated profiling package plus 'Tachyon', a high-frequency statistical sampling profiler; typing adds PEP 728 TypedDict typed extra items, PEP 747 TypeForm, and PEP 800 disjoint bases.
summary: Python 3.15.0 final shipped on 2026-10-09, built from 5,643 commits by 1,012 contributors since 3.14. The release adds language and builtin features (PEP 661 sentinel, PEP 814 frozendict, PEP 810 explicit lazy imports, PEP 686 UTF-8 default encoding, PEP 798 unpacking in comprehensions) and upgrades the still-experimental JIT, which the team reports at 7-8% geomean speedup on x86-64 Linux over the standard interpreter and 11-12% on AArch64 macOS over the tail-calling interpreter (no methodology given). Two packaging defaults change: macOS binaries now install free-threading support by default and Windows 64-bit binaries use the tail-calling interpreter, while PEP 831 turns on frame pointers by default. Typing gains PEP 728, PEP 747 TypeForm, and PEP 800 disjoint bases; the stdlib adds a PEP 799 profiling package and the Tachyon sampling profiler. A documented regression: tkinter/IDLE dialogs hang on macOS 27.0 due to an OS behavior change affecting all current Tk versions, tracked in issue #158053.
novelty: JIT compiler now 7-12% faster, lazy imports, frozendict builtin
audience: Python engineers planning upgrades and library maintainers tracking C API/typing changes

title: Superlite: A Faster Alternatie to Superpowers
why: If your Claude Code builds crawl, the bottleneck is usually serial dispatch and per-step approval prompts, not model latency: this plugin cut a 177-test benchmark build to 16.1 minutes with zero human stops by parallelizing tasks and gating rules in hook code.
notes: superlite is a Claude Code plugin (iha2/superlite) forked from 'superpowers', reusing its plugin layout, session-start hook, and lifecycle skills; the author warns against enabling both in one session because they share skill names and both inject startup context.

It collapses the author's measured 8-12 human gates per feature into one batch of up to four questions plus a single design-and-plan sign-off; after that it only halts for destructive, outward-facing, or security-sensitive actions (e.g., it won't push to main unprompted), and never pushes or merges without you.

Work is a task graph keyed on file ownership and declared input/output interfaces; independent tasks run concurrently, peaking at 18 agents at once (21 total) on the benchmark, with first agents building ~3 minutes in.

Model tiers: Opus orchestrates and does a final review-only pass (barred from editing code), Sonnet implements and reviews, Haiku handles small fully-specified off-critical-path tasks, and tiered fix-only agents apply findings.

Rules are enforced by hooks, not prompts: one blocks the coordinator from editing project code, another converts foreground pytest/npm test into background runs so tests never block, plans must pass `lint --stable` before work starts, and hooks log per-agent tokens/cost/time with a soft budget alert at 70% of cap.

Self-reported benchmark (static site generator plus spreadsheet engine, 177 hidden tests, run on Opus): 16.1 min and 177/177, versus superpowers stock 33.6 min mean and orchestrated 23.5 min mean (52% and 31% less); author concedes this is one run of the current build against earlier runs on the same machine, 'a strong hint rather than peer-reviewed science.'
summary: superlite is a Claude Code plugin, forked from the 'superpowers' workflow, built for autonomous rather than step-by-step collaborative development. It replaces superpowers' 8-12 per-feature human approval gates with a single batch of questions and one plan sign-off, then runs unattended except for destructive, outward-facing, or security-sensitive actions. Builds are structured as a task graph partitioned by file ownership and declared interfaces, so independent tasks execute in parallel (up to 18 concurrent agents in the benchmark), with models assigned by tier: Opus coordinates and does a final review-only pass, Sonnet implements and reviews, Haiku handles small mechanical tasks, and separate fix-only agents apply review findings. Operational constraints are enforced by hooks rather than prompts, including blocking the coordinator from editing code, forcing tests into background runs, and requiring plans to pass a lint check before work begins. On a self-run benchmark (a static site generator plus spreadsheet engine scored by 177 hidden tests), superlite completed in 16.1 minutes with all tests passing and no human stops, versus superpowers at 33.6 minutes stock and 23.5 minutes orchestrated. The author presents the numbers as a single current-build run against earlier same-machine runs, explicitly calling it a strong hint rather than rigorous evidence.
novelty: parallel multi-model agent orchestration, single approval gate vs per-step

title: Beyond Maliciousness: Static and Runtime Attack-Surface Profiling of Agent Skills
why: Install an agent skill and you grant it your session's privileges: across 6,309 marketplace listings, 70% carry at least one elevated capability and half can run a shell, almost none of it visible at install time.
notes: Methodology: two-phase profiling of 6,309 listings from two marketplaces (ClawHub, skillsmp), combining whole-bundle static analysis and dependency provenance checks with instrumented sandbox execution plus model-based assessment of traces; listings were selected for execution without conditioning on any prior threat signal.

Capability prevalence (static+runtime measured): 50% show shell-execution capability, 35% filesystem read, 31% filesystem write, 31% network egress, 13% credential access; 7 in 10 carry at least one elevated capability.

Skills are Markdown instruction documents that run with the authority of the session that loaded them; installing grants standing to direct the agent rather than new OS privilege, and that grant is what the paper quantifies.

The permission model is described as 'close to inert': frontmatter only pre-approves tools to suppress confirmation prompts, it does not restrict reach; its vocabulary cannot even express credential or environment access, and nothing checks declarations against the bundle.

Declaration gap: of 6,061 parseable listings only 770 declare anything, and 59% of declaring listings understate actual capability; ClawHub declares roughly 2x as often as skillsmp yet under-declares on 88% of its declarations vs 31% for skillsmp.

Conclusion: marketplace triage cannot rest on declared permissions and must rest on what the bundle can do; capability-oriented attack-surface profiling is framed as a complement to maliciousness detection, not a replacement.
summary: This preprint audits the attack surface of "agent skills," Markdown instruction documents that a tool-using agent reads and then acts on with the privileges of the loading session. Using a two-phase methodology (whole-bundle static analysis and dependency provenance plus instrumented sandbox execution with model-based trace assessment), the authors profile 6,309 listings from two marketplaces, ClawHub and skillsmp, choosing listings for execution without conditioning on prior risk signals. They report that 50% show shell-execution capability, 35% filesystem read, 31% each filesystem write and network egress, and 13% credential access, with 70% carrying at least one elevated capability, none of which is visible at install time. The existing permission model only suppresses confirmation prompts rather than restricting reach: of 6,061 parseable listings only 770 declare anything, the frontmatter vocabulary cannot express credential or environment access, and 59% of declaring listings understate what their bundle can do (ClawHub under-declares on 88% of declarations vs 31% for skillsmp). The authors argue marketplace triage must rest on measured bundle capability rather than self-declaration, positioning capability-oriented profiling as a complement to maliciousness detection. Numbers are self-reported by the authors; the abstract does not describe false-positive rates or validation of the capability-detection pipeline.
novelty: first large-scale capability audit of agent-skill marketplaces vs self-declared permissions
audience: engineers building or securing agentic coding tools and skill marketplaces

title: Show HN: Esp32sim – Run ESP32 firmware in the browser
why: You can boot an unmodified ESP-IDF firmware image through the real mask ROM into FreeRTOS in a browser tab, debug it with trace/break/watch, and even hit the real network over a virtual WPA2 AP, with no board, no cloud, and no patched firmware.
notes: Covers four SoCs: classic ESP32 (dual Xtensa LX6), ESP32-S3 (dual LX7 @240MHz), ESP32-C3 (RISC-V RV32IMC @160MHz), and ESP32-C6 (RISC-V RV32IMAC @160MHz). Each boots real mask ROM to 2nd-stage bootloader to FreeRTOS to app with no stubs or patched firmware.

Speed differs by target: S3 uses a block interpreter plus AArch64 JIT at a reported ~150-240 Minsn/s (roughly 30x real time on hello_world); C3 and C6 use a plain interpreter with no block cache or JIT yet. S3 and C3/C6 are labeled 'mature' and 'draft' respectively.

Hardware validation is explicitly not cycle-exact: S3 checked in JTAG lock-step (reportedly 3000-8000 steps, 0 PC divergence after masking window exceptions and resyncing CCOUNT delay loops); C3 and C6 validated by console diff (205/208 and 203/204 lines identical over three boot cycles, the differences being the ROM 'Saved PC:' line). The author says these comparisons each found five emulator bugs, including a device-command race and a reset-time cycle counter bug.

A virtual WiFi AP lets the unmodified Espressif WiFi blob do scan, auth, association and the WPA2-PSK four-way handshake; a virtual network behind it provides DHCP/ARP/ICMP/DNS/SNTP, and --net nat relays guest TCP/UDP over host sockets for real HTTPS. In-browser WASM builds have no NAT since the browser has no sockets. Reported decoder checks: 977k/161k/126k instructions with 0 mismatches, from earlier manual runs excluded from CI.

Architecture shares most of the SoC across chips: C3 and C6 reuse the S3's UART, USB-Serial/JTAG, timers, GPIO, SPI flash controller, GDMA and SHA/AES/RSA models; only the CPU crates are genuinely separate. The C6 adds an 802.15.4 MAC that answers energy scans and, via --cooja, drives as an external Cooja-NG mote in lock-step with emulated MSP430 nodes.

MIT licensed (copyright Joakim Eriksson, Alice, Mattia Fiumara), written from ESP-IDF register headers, the RISC-V spec and the C3/C6 TRMs; QEMU was consulted for instruction semantics only, no code copied. Live demos run Linux 6.11 on the S3, a SID player, and a '4-bit transformer' fish-steering demo.
summary: esp32sim is an MIT-licensed, instruction-level emulator for four Espressif SoCs across both of its CPU architectures: the classic ESP32 and S3 (Xtensa) and the C3 and C6 (RISC-V). Each target boots the real mask ROM, real 2nd-stage bootloader, and an unmodified ESP-IDF application image through FreeRTOS, with enough of the SoC modeled (GPIO, UART, timers, SPI flash, DMA, crypto, displays, WiFi/802.15.4 MACs) to run full projects end to end, and the whole thing compiles to WebAssembly to run client-side in a browser with no accounts. The S3 path is the most mature, using a block interpreter plus AArch64 JIT at a reported ~150-240 Minsn/s; the C3 and C6 are labeled draft and use a plain interpreter. A virtual WiFi access point with WPA2, DHCP/DNS/NTP and host NAT lets unmodified firmware reach the real network over HTTPS without root or a tun device. The author validates against physical boards by different methods (S3 via JTAG lock-step, C3/C6 via console diffs of 205/208 and 203/204 identical lines) and is explicit that this is not cycle-exact: comparisons normalize window exceptions and resync delay loops, and found five emulator bugs each. Most peripheral models are shared across chips, with only the CPU crates genuinely separate.
novelty: full-system ESP32 emulation booting real unmodified firmware in-browser via WASM
audience: embedded/firmware engineers working with ESP32 who want CI/testing without hardware

title: Mac at Any Scale
why: If you run iOS CI or coding agents that need a Mac, this is the operational playbook for renting macOS at scale: 4 Gbps guest networking, two-VM-per-host limits, and multi-hundred-GB Xcode images distributed BitTorrent-style.
notes: Namespace racks MacBook Pros, not Mac Minis, because Mac Minis ordered in January 2026 arrived in July and lag on CPU updates (Mini skipped M5 for 10 months, then jumped to M6 first); each laptop gets an IP KVM, an external 10G NIC, and four cables, totaling 48 cables plus 12 Ethernet plus KVM wiring per shelf.

Unexpected failure modes: HDMI cables (not MagSafe) were the least reliable connector, to the point they bought out Amazon's entire supply of a good one; FileVault reboot prompts expire after 5 minutes on both KVM screen and Tahoe's SSH remote unlock, forcing a physical reboot-and-race, with `fdesetup authrestart` offered as a workaround that keeps the disk unlocked.

Built on Apple's Virtualization framework (compared to Firecracker), not the lower-level Hypervisor framework, which cannot run macOS; Apple caps macOS to two VMs per physical host regardless of hardware, so even a 24-core/192GB machine is sliced only in half (e.g. 6/12-core instances on 14-core Minis).

Guest networking is routed through a gVisor userspace TCP/IP stack to enforce per-customer policies on untrusted code; every packet crosses an IPC boundary between the VMM and host processes, capping throughput at a claimed 4 Gbps upstream (measured via Fast.com), below line rate.

VM images reach 2 TB across macOS versions, iOS runtimes, and Xcode betas; Namespace stores them sparse and as layered shallow copies in its OCI registry, distributes blocks peer-to-peer (BitTorrent-inspired, but among trusted peers), and materializes them to each node's local SSD using APFS holes and clonefile/`cp -c` rather than slower NBD-backed disks.

A caveat flagged in the text: installing an Xcode beta bumps global CoreDevice/CoreSimulator versions and breaks stable Xcode on the same system, forcing separate image variants with and without pre-release Xcode.
summary: Namespace, a cloud infrastructure provider, describes how it runs macOS at scale for customers building and testing iOS apps, which require a Mac, the iOS Simulator, and a recent Xcode to ship to the App Store. Because Mac Mini supply chains were delayed (ordered January, delivered July 2026) and lagged on CPU updates, the company racked MacBook Pros instead, wiring each with an IP KVM, an external 10G NIC, and custom heat-wicking holders, and solving surprise problems like unreliable HDMI cables and FileVault unlock prompts that expire after 5 minutes. macOS instances run as VMs on Apple's Virtualization framework (akin to Firecracker), which caps hosts at two macOS VMs each, so machines are sliced in half. Untrusted guest traffic is processed through a gVisor userspace network stack, which incurs IPC roundtrips and limits throughput to a self-reported 4 Gbps upstream. Multi-terabyte VM images (driven by large iOS runtimes and multiple Xcode versions) are stored sparse and layered in an OCI registry, distributed peer-to-peer in BitTorrent fashion, and materialized to local SSDs using APFS sparse files and clonefile. The post notes incoming M5/M6 Minis and Studios are far simpler to manage (built-in 10G, auto power-on, full MDM) and teases custom single-cable USB-C hardware and possibly racking phones next.
novelty: operational details of racking MacBooks (not Minis) as cloud CI infra
audience: infra/devops engineers running CI fleets and iOS build pipelines

title: Decompiling Fast Food Tycoon 2: Drawing the World
why: An LLM agent, given Ghidra output, live process memory, and a patched message handler, reconstructed a 2001 game's entire rendering and simulation logic without ever editing the executable on disk, a concrete template for agent-driven reverse engineering.
notes: Toolchain: Ghidra decompiled fastfood2.exe's 4,046 functions into ~9.5MB of C-like text (addresses, field offsets, constants, calls), loaded into SQLite and wrapped with a decomp_index.py script for grep, callers, and string queries; the author drove a self-described GPT-6.1 Sol Medium agentic loop.

Live inspection: the agent used Windows ReadProcessMemory to read running values (cash, camera position, selected building) and traced the decompiled functions that wrote those addresses; it patched the Windows message handler to inject clicks and camera moves on the game's own UI thread, leaving the on-disk binary untouched. A UI crawler mapped the remaining unknown controls.

Renderer: dirty-region repainting limits redraws, cells are visited diagonally/isometrically across multiple passes, and hidden characters are kept visible by marking their shape with a temporary pixel value, then outlining covered body parts (yellow) and thought icons (white). Each pixel stores a 16-bit color plus a separate lighting byte, combined with a dither pattern only at final draw.

Lighting: a 25-entry hourly table ranges from 70 at night to 251 at day; lamp on/off thresholds stagger via `light <= 160 + (lamp.id & 7)`, so default standard lamps switch on ~18:25-18:30 and off ~05:35-05:40. Pizzerias use paired sprite files, a light mask (.m.spr) kept per-pixel as the brighter of two values and night window colors (.l.spr), so signs and windows stay lit while the building darkens.

Simulation details (author claims from decompiled code): citizen schedules persist across days rather than resetting; walker speeds differ (errand boy 27px/s, tourist 16.2px/s, celebrity 13.8px/s); pizza scoring splits each pie into 24 regions, checks topping symmetry and ingredient pairings per customer group, and runs a plagiarism check on ingredient weights that flags copied recipes as 'not original', costing +30 taste points for yuppies/goths/tourists and +5 for big shots.

Provenance notes: internal strings and animation names are mostly German; a config file labels the game 'Pizza3' (Init-File fuer Pizza3-Stadt); the title is Fast Food Tycoon 2, known in Europe as Pizza Connection 2. The post's generated images reuse the game's own decompiled fonts.
summary: A developer describes decompiling the 2001 isometric business sim Fast Food Tycoon 2 (European name Pizza Connection 2) by running an LLM agentic loop over Ghidra output. Ghidra turned the executable's 4,046 functions into ~9.5MB of C-like text, stored in SQLite and queried through a custom index script; the agent correlated live memory read via ReadProcessMemory with the code that modified those values, and controlled the game by patching the Windows message handler to post commands to its UI thread without altering the binary on disk. The write-up reconstructs the renderer in detail: dirty-region repainting, diagonal multi-pass draw order, a temporary-pixel trick that outlines characters hidden behind walls, and a per-pixel 16-bit color plus separate lighting byte combined with dithering at final output. Lighting runs off a 25-entry hourly brightness table (70 night to 251 day) with lamps staggered by object-ID bitmasking and pizzerias using paired light-mask and night-color sprite files that keep windows and signs lit. The author also documents simulation quirks drawn from the code: persistent daily citizen schedules with stereotyped allocations, differing walker speeds, and a pizza scoring system that divides each pizza into 24 regions, checks symmetry and ingredient pairings, and runs a plagiarism check by ingredient weight. All technical specifics are the author's reading of the decompiled code and self-reported; no external verification or full methodology for the agent loop is provided.
novelty: agentic LLM-driven decompilation reverse-engineering a 2001 game's renderer
audience: systems/graphics programmers and reverse-engineering enthusiasts

title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
why: If the self-reported numbers hold, you can quantize a 122B-parameter model to 4-bit weights and activations in 64 minutes on a single 32.5GB GPU, with only 2.3% inference overhead over plain MXFP4.
notes: MACaQ is an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently, avoiding the cross-layer basis-transform propagation that other recent methods require.

Each layer gets a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform applied to activations online at inference; the inverse transforms are folded into the weights. Keeping transforms online removes cross-layer dependencies and permits a streaming implementation holding only one layer in memory at a time.
Flip-Refinement is a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent step that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values, improving over round-to-nearest.

Reported results: 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM; lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, matching their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11x less quantization time; a 122B model quantized in 64 minutes using 32.5GB GPU RAM.
The same layer-local design is applied to an image diffusion model without architecture-specific changes, which the authors offer as evidence of generality.
All numbers are author-reported from the arXiv abstract; no independent evaluation, methodology detail, or baseline configuration is provided in the excerpt.
summary: MACaQ is a post-training quantization method for MXFP4 W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) that quantizes each linear layer independently, in contrast to methods that propagate basis transforms across layers. It applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform to activations online at inference time and absorbs the inverse transforms into the weights; because transforms stay online rather than being fused across layers, quantization can stream through the model with only one layer resident in memory. A Flip-Refinement step uses Hessian-aware coordinate descent to move individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values, improving on round-to-nearest. The authors report 2.3% end-to-end inference overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM, lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, matching their best Llama-3-8B perplexity in 11x less quantization time, and quantization of a 122B-parameter model in 64 minutes using 32.5GB of GPU RAM. The method is also applied unmodified to an image diffusion model. All figures are self-reported in the abstract and lack independent verification or methodology detail.
novelty: layer-local online Hadamard quantization avoids cross-layer calibration
audience: ML engineers deploying quantized LLMs/diffusion models at scale

title: Switch Lowering in GCC
why: If you have ever profiled a hot dispatch loop and wondered why GCC emitted branches instead of a jump table, this reverse-engineers the exact thresholds that decide it, down to a ratio of 8 at -O3 versus 2 at -Os.
notes: The jump-table heuristic compares jump-table entries against comparisons, not raw case labels: GCC merges contiguous case ranges first, so a 20-label switch spanning 0-87 (88 entries) lowers to comparisons because it reduces to 10 comparisons and 10*8 < 88 fails the ratio test.

The ratio is set by optimization goal: 8 entries-per-comparison when optimizing for speed (-O1/2/3/fast), 2 when optimizing for size (-Os). Both bitset and jump-table lowering use dynamic programming to minimize the number of clusters.

For small, non-contiguous value sets GCC emits a bitset plus the x86 bt (bit test) instruction against a constant (e.g. 2753205), where set bits are the ASCII case values each offset by 48; the author notes bitset lowering does not transfer to Clang.

GCC detects dense subsets inside sparse switches: an outlier like case 100 gets its own cmp/branch while cases 1-5 still get a jump table. Jump tables below case_values_threshold (defaults to 5 on modern x64/Arm64) are pruned as unprofitable.

Missed optimization flagged by the author: in a sparse-but-regular switch (sparse_8), GCC does not divide x by 8 before indexing, emitting a comparison tree instead. The fallback tree is built by splitting labels into equal-probability halves, using PGO or __builtin_expect_with_probability.
The work is attributed to the pass_lower_switch pass calling analyze_switch_statement, observed under GCC -O3 from disassembly; findings are the author's reverse-engineering, not GCC documentation.
summary: A reverse-engineering walkthrough of how GCC lowers C switch statements, derived from -O3 disassembly and annotated GCC source. GCC chooses among three strategies: a jump table (indirect jump through an address array), a bitset test using the bt instruction for small non-contiguous value sets, and a binary decision tree as fallback. The jump-table decision uses dynamic programming and a ratio heuristic comparing jump-table entries to the number of comparisons after contiguous ranges are merged, with the ratio being 8 for speed and 2 for size; jump tables smaller than case_values_threshold (default 5) are rejected. GCC can isolate dense subsets within sparse switches, emitting a table for the cluster and separate branches for outliers. The author notes missed optimizations, such as failing to divide the index by a stride in a regular-but-sparse case, and that all techniques except bitset lowering carry over to Clang.
novelty: reverse-engineers GCC's switch-lowering heuristics via disassembly
audience: systems/compiler engineers optimizing hot-path switch statements

title: The Commodore 64 hardware simulator: break chips and pins, see the results
why: If you repair vintage boards, this lets you reproduce a specific fault, lifting A7 on the color RAM, shorting a pin to +5V, pulling a chip, and read the resulting screen garbage before you desolder anything, so you touch the fewest chips in the most logical order.
notes: Simulates the Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 motherboard pin by pin from bwack's KiCad replica netlist: 216 parts, their pads, and 249 nets (converted by tools/kicad2c.py).

Cycle-accurate 6510/VIC-II/CIA/SID cores come from floooh's chips library (via c64-llm, zlib); antirez added pin-level models for the DRAMs, ROMs, color RAM, glue logic, and the PLA with its real 82S100 equations (read out by Mark Smith and Marko Mäkelä).

Not an emulator for play: it runs at 31% of real C64 speed on an Apple M3 Max, 39% on a Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495, and 48% on an Apple M5 Max, because every pin of every chip is simulated. Each half cycle settles in three steps: row address, /RAS falls, /CAS falls.

Electrical model: strongest drive wins a net, equal fighting drives show contention (low wins, magenta on the probe), undriven nets hold charge then drift to ~1.4V with TTL loads or toward 0V with MOS loads. A chip without GND floats its outputs high; a CMOS chip keeps running on phantom power through its pins' protection diodes. Noise is seeded so runs are reproducible.

Scriptable: CLI fault syntax REF:what or REF.PIN:what (U17:removed, U21.14:gnd, R51:open), --headless with --text reading the screen as a person would plus --shot PNG, timed --at faults, and tests/faults.sh covers 31 common faults whose expected symptoms were written down before the simulator ran. Author warns a matching symptom is a clue, not proof.

Stated limits: floating/power thresholds, drift times, and crosstalk are hand-tuned guesses in src/sim.c; video output, SID filter, PSU, and dot-clock PLL are not simulated; in-chip faults (bad DRAM cells, slow parts) and net-to-net bridges are planned but not implemented.
summary: c64-hw-sim is a pin-level simulator of the Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 motherboard by antirez, built to diagnose faults rather than play games. It combines floooh's cycle-accurate 6510/VIC-II/CIA/SID cores (zlib) with new pin-level models of the DRAMs, ROMs, color RAM, glue logic, and the PLA's real equations, driven by bwack's KiCad replica netlist (216 parts, 249 nets). The user can lift a chip leg, short a pin to GND or +5V, pull a chip, or open a resistor, and observe the computed result on the monitor, keyboard, and an on-screen oscilloscope; the garbage shown is derived from the circuit and net-level electrical rules (drive strength, contention, charge drift to ~1.4V or 0V, phantom CMOS power via protection diodes), not hand-authored. It runs well below real time (31-48% on an M3 Max, Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495, and M5 Max) and supports headless, scripted fault injection with text and screenshot output, plus a test suite of 31 faults with symptoms documented beforehand. The author is explicit that a matching symptom is a clue rather than proof, that floating and power thresholds are tuned guesses, and that the video output, SID filter, PSU, dot-clock PLL, in-chip faults, and net bridges are not modeled. It runs on macOS and Linux via OpenGL, sokol, and nuklear.
novelty: pin-level C64 motherboard simulator for fault diagnosis, not emulation
audience: retrocomputing hobbyists and hardware repair engineers

title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
why: A text-to-image model good enough to draw 258 Hacker News upvotes was trained end-to-end on 64 H100s for about $21K with Apache 2.0 weights, giving builders a reproducible recipe for pixel-space diffusion that skips the VAE entirely.
notes: P-JiT is a 2B-parameter DiT operating directly in pixel space, with no VAE; the lab claims this lets it compress a 512 image into the token count previously used for 256, and converge in 11x fewer samples than their prior Linum v2.

Text conditioning comes from a frozen Qwen3.5-4B read at its three full-attention layers (7, 15, 27); text and image each pass two single-modality refiner blocks before merging into 22 shared DiT blocks. Image is patched 32x32 into a 1024-dim space.

To fight weak gradients in early DiT blocks, intermediate readout heads after blocks 10 and 16 predict quarter- and half-resolution clean images, plus a DINOv3-L alignment readout at block 5; total loss combines readout MSE, PixelREPA cosine distance, final-head MSE, and LPIPS perceptual loss.

Training: 610M samples at 512 (297,985 steps) then 50M at 1024, global batch 2,048, Muon on 2D matrices plus AdamW elsewhere, noise-schedule curriculum (LogitNormal 0.8,0.8 high-noise for first 80M samples then widened), EMA from 100M samples, RoPE interpolation across the resolution jump. Hardware: 64x H100 (8 nodes), bf16, FSDP2.

Stated limits, self-reported: no rendered-text capability (text/infographic data filtered out as irrelevant to their animation goal), and weak on full bodies, many entities, multi-person interactions, and world knowledge; they attribute this to size and suggest a 7B model plus more post-training would help.

Framing caveat: this is a 2-person lab's proof-of-concept toward a from-scratch video model, not a benchmarked release; image-quality claims are visual and self-assessed, with no quantitative comparisons (FID, human-eval numbers) provided.
summary: Linum, a two-person research lab, released Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT), a 2B-parameter text-to-image diffusion transformer trained from scratch for roughly $21K and published under Apache 2.0. The design's central bet is to drop the VAE and run diffusion directly in pixel space, which the lab says enables more aggressive token compression (a 512 image in the tokens formerly used for 256) and 11x faster convergence than their prior Linum v2. Architecturally, text (from a frozen Qwen3.5-4B read at layers 7, 15, 27) and image streams each pass two refiner blocks before merging into 22 shared DiT blocks; intermediate readout heads predicting low-resolution images and a DINOv3-L alignment readout counter weak early-layer gradients. Training used 610M samples at 512 then 50M at 1024 on 64 H100s, with a noise-schedule curriculum, Muon plus AdamW optimizers, EMA, and RoPE interpolation for the resolution transition, followed by a Finite Difference Flow Optimization post-training variant with human-in-the-loop judges. The model cannot render text (that data was filtered out) and struggles with full bodies, crowds, multi-person scenes, and world knowledge. The release is positioned as a proof-of-concept en route to a from-scratch video model; quality claims are self-reported with no quantitative benchmarks given.
novelty: pixel-space diffusion model skips VAE, trained for ~$20K
audience: ML researchers/engineers working on efficient generative image/video models

title: AI, Lean, and the Future of Formal Verification, with Lean Creator Leo de Moura
why: Frontier models can now translate code in any language into Lean and write machine-checked proofs, so verification that was too hand-labor-intensive for industry is cheap enough to point at your own codebase, and the editing shifts from code to specifications.
notes: De Moura (creator of Lean, VP/Distinguished Scientist at AWS, Chief Architect of the Lean Focused Research Organization) frames the trust boundary: to trust a Lean result you only need to trust the kernel; Lean ships two verified checkers with a third coming, and a kernel 'arena' (arena.lean-lang.org) benchmarks independent implementations written in Rust, C#, Haskell, TeX, COBOL, and Fortran.

Scale claim: Mathlib took humans ~10 years to reach 2.5M lines; AI-written Lean proofs now reach 50M lines, and Anthropic's Fermat's Last Theorem proof is cited at 13M lines (self-reported figures, no methodology given). De Moura notes proofs are refactorable data, not static, and groups have cut the FLT proof roughly in half while the machine check still passes.

Verification vs. testing: testing (including AI-generated property-based tests) shows the presence of bugs, not their absence; a Lean proof covers all inputs. Example: Kim Morrison ported zlib to Lean and proved compress-then-decompress round-trips losslessly at any compression level.

Rust path is concrete today: Aeneas verifies Rust against Lean and is used by Microsoft's SymCrypt crypto library team. For other languages, de Moura says AI builds a Lean model of the code; the open caveat is model faithfulness, checked via differential testing (running model and program to find discrepancies). Claude Code's Boris reportedly had Claude find and file real bug PRs this way without knowing Lean.

Two named failure modes persist: the requirement gap (spec X vs. what the customer wants, X') and the model gap (idealized conditions vs. production). On Navier-Stokes the problem statement was human-curated and sound, but OpenAI's natural-language and Lean proofs mismatched (e.g., a fourth- vs. fifth-derivative assumption); de Moura argues the Verso Blueprint tool, which aligns LaTeX/natural language with Lean, would have caught it.
summary: In a Data Exchange podcast, Lean creator Leo de Moura (AWS; Lean FRO) argues that as AI makes code generation easy, machine-checked formal verification becomes the needed complement to testing, which can find bugs but not prove their absence. He describes Lean as both a language and proof assistant whose trust reduces to a small kernel, now backed by two verified checkers (a third coming) and independent kernels in languages including Rust, Haskell, TeX, and COBOL, tracked at a public arena. The change he credits is frontier models gaining autoformalization: they can translate code in any language into Lean models and write proofs, citing claimed scales of 50M-line AI proofs and Anthropic's 13M-line Fermat's Last Theorem proof against Mathlib's human-built 2.5M lines. Concrete examples include Kim Morrison's zlib port proving lossless round-trip compression, Aeneas verifying Rust (used by Microsoft's SymCrypt), and Claude finding real bugs in Claude Code via generated Lean models. De Moura flags open caveats: model faithfulness (addressed via differential testing), the requirement gap and model gap, and the Navier-Stokes case where informal and Lean proofs mismatched on a derivative assumption. He predicts engineering work shifts toward writing and refining formal specifications, with specs becoming the maintained source of truth. The figures and capability claims are self-reported in interview and not accompanied by methodology.
novelty: Lean creator's view on AI-generated code needing formal verification, not just testing
audience: engineers/researchers interested in formal verification, theorem proving, and AI code trust

title: Monitor Accuracy Isn't the Answer: A Decision-Value Framework for Evaluating AI Agent Restart Monitors
why: If you build agent harnesses that restart stuck runs on a monitor's signal, a 90%-accurate monitor can still cost you success: the same detector swings from a 5-point loss to a 35-point gain depending only on how much budget the replacement run has left.
notes: Core analytic claim: using an exact alarm-to-action identity for a clean restart with zero monitoring overhead, a monitor held at 90% accuracy ranges from a 5-point success-rate loss to a 35-point gain, driven entirely by the replacement attempt's residual-budget success probability. Accuracy, TPR, and FPR alone do not determine whether restarting helps.

Two proposed evaluation tools: a decision-sufficiency criterion (binary-action specialization of Blackwell's comparison of experiments) that tests whether a progress representation or context compression keeps the information needed to choose optimally between restart and continue, independent of trace-reconstruction fidelity; and a finite-sample, model-free decision audit using simultaneous binomial intervals over existing traces (no extra model calls) that certifies 'restart', 'continue', or 'abstain'.
Empirical setup: 194 externally evaluated model executions on 19 selected SymPy issues from SWE-bench Verified, with a retrospective audit of 130 traces.

Findings undercut restart gains: a 2.29-point apparent restart gain traced to a single surviving failed attempt; a 42.29-point loss on a second model; no positive replication of the initial gain on prospective task cohorts.
Certification failure: zero of 103 live comparisons met the paper's bar for confidently preferring restart over continue under its stated sampling assumptions.

Caveats to flag: results are self-reported in a single arXiv preprint, scoped to SymPy issues and a small issue count (19), and the clean-idealized analysis assumes an independent restart with zero monitoring overhead.
summary: The paper argues that classification metrics (accuracy, true-positive and false-positive rates) do not determine whether restarting a stuck AI agent improves task success. Using an exact alarm-to-action identity for an independent clean restart with no monitoring overhead, the authors show analytically that a monitor fixed at 90% accuracy can produce anywhere from a 5-point loss to a 35-point gain in success rate, depending solely on the replacement attempt's residual-budget success probability. They propose two decision-oriented evaluation methods: a decision-sufficiency criterion derived from Blackwell's comparison of experiments, and a finite-sample, model-free audit using simultaneous binomial intervals over existing traces that returns 'restart', 'continue', or 'abstain'. Empirically, across 194 externally evaluated executions on 19 SymPy issues from SWE-bench Verified (130 traces audited retrospectively), a 2.29-point apparent restart gain traced to one surviving failed attempt, a second model showed a 42.29-point loss, no positive replication appeared on prospective cohorts, and none of 103 live comparisons met the certification bar. The authors conclude that monitors should be judged on recovery opportunity, decision value, and statistical support rather than classification performance.
novelty: decision-value framework shows restart-monitor accuracy doesn't predict usefulness
audience: engineers building or evaluating AI agent monitoring/restart systems

title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents
why: Coding agents approve shell commands from text alone, so a dangerous payload hidden inside an invoked tool slips past: running each command in a snapshotted sandbox first cut the harmful-outcome rate on that hidden-payload benchmark from at least 35.3% to 7.8%.
notes: Caper pre-executes each proposed shell command in a snapshotted sandbox, hands an independent approver a bounded report of the observed effects, commits allowed commands, and rolls back blocked ones with a reason the agent can use to recover.
On SABER it reports a 6.7% harmful-outcome rate versus at least 14.8% across six existing systems (rule-based checkers, guardrail models, deployed permission classifiers).

The authors built YoloFS-Ext, a benchmark where harmful behavior is hidden inside invoked tools rather than the command text; Caper scores 7.8% harmful-outcome versus at least 35.3% for baselines, the gap the text-only approach misses.
False-positive cost on YoloFS-Ext is low: Caper blocks 1.0% of the safe twins of the dangerous tasks.
The stated contrast is with systems that assess effects post-hoc from observed file changes, leaving the final call to the agent or a human after the command has already run.

All numbers are self-reported in the paper; the abstract gives no detail on sandbox fidelity, runtime cost of pre-execution, or how commands with external side effects (network, non-rollbackable state) are handled.
summary: Caper is a consequence-aware approval mechanism for autonomous coding agents that decides whether a shell command may run by actually executing it first. Instead of judging the request and command text like rule-based checkers, guardrail models, and permission classifiers do, Caper pre-executes each command in a snapshotted sandbox, gives an independent approver a bounded report of the observed effects, then commits allowed commands and rolls back blocked ones with an actionable reason. The authors report the lowest harmful-outcome rate on the SABER benchmark, 6.7% versus at least 14.8% for six existing systems. They also introduce YoloFS-Ext, a benchmark where harmful behavior is hidden inside invoked tools rather than visible in the command, where Caper reaches 7.8% versus at least 35.3% for baselines while blocking only 1.0% of the safe twins of dangerous tasks. The results are self-reported, and the abstract does not address sandbox fidelity, pre-execution latency, or commands with irreversible external side effects.
novelty: pre-executes commands in sandbox before approval, not just text analysis
audience: engineers building or securing autonomous coding-agent pipelines

title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
why: Static CTF-style agent evals saturate; this proposes a head-to-head format where two agents attack and defend the same evolving services at once, which is closer to how offensive/defensive AI tooling actually gets stressed.
notes: Design: two agents compete in isolated sandboxes under identical rules, acting concurrently as attacker and defender over services that change across multiple rounds, converting static targets into evolving semi-open challenges.

Scale of the study: 12 frontier LLM agents, 40 challenges, 466 matches; authors claim the format separates models where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling (claim, no methodology or model names given in the abstract).
An automated agentic pipeline generates, reviews, and validates new environments to keep the benchmark from saturating; the pipeline itself is not described or validated in the provided text.

Scoring: a 'dynamical model' maps pairwise match dynamics into unified multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities, addressing the difficulty of quantifying pairwise contests (mechanism not detailed in the abstract).

Reported emergent behaviors: agents planting backdoors for later rounds, one writing its own packet sniffer to watch the opponent, and defenders patching one hole while missing the next and certifying repairs on stale evidence (anecdotal, self-reported).
arXiv preprint (cs.CR); no code, data, or reproducibility details confirmed in the provided text, and all capability results are authors' own.
summary: CyberArena is a proposed benchmark for evaluating AI agents in live, symmetric cyber combat rather than against static isolated targets. Two agents run in isolated sandboxes under identical rules, acting as both attacker and defender over continuously changing services across multiple rounds, testing speed and precision at discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. An automated agentic pipeline is used to generate, review, and validate new environments to resist saturation, and a 'dynamical model' converts pairwise match dynamics into multidimensional offensive, defensive, and domain-specific scores. The authors evaluate 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches and claim the format separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines plateau. They report emergent behaviors including agents planting backdoors for future rounds, one writing a custom packet sniffer to observe its opponent, and defenders patching incompletely or certifying fixes on stale evidence. This is an arXiv preprint; the abstract gives no methodology detail for the scoring model, no model names, and the capability and behavior claims are self-reported.
novelty: live symmetric attack-defense benchmark replacing static CTF-style eval
audience: AI security researchers evaluating autonomous offensive/defensive agents

title: RPKI Now Protects 70% of Internet Routes, Up from 54% a Year Ago
why: If you still read RPKI country stats as raw percentages, you are misjudging risk: weighting by how many vantage points actually see a route collapses Spain's alarming 28.2% invalid share to 0.057%, and shows invalid routes die at a median of 2 collectors instead of ~595.
notes: RPKI-valid routed prefixes rose 54.0% to 70.3% in a year (counted by addresses, 53.1% to 65.0%); China drove nearly 60% of the address-weighted gain, going from 3.7% to 83.0% of its IPv4 in valid routes, most of it after December 2025. Outside China the rise was only 5.2 points.

Filtering is working: valid prefixes reach a median 596 RIPE RIS/RouteViews peers, unknown 595, but invalid just 2; 71% of origin-mismatch invalids reach a single vantage point. Internet Society Pulse put RPKI-related BGP update volume under 1% in August, so it isn't destabilizing routing.

RPKI checks origin only, not path. The Aug 28 2026 Hetzner incident: a forged AS24940 origin on 162.55.80.0/24 passed validation because Hetzner's ROA covered the surrounding /16 with maxLength down to /24; attackers got a real TLS cert and served a malicious Virtualizor update (per Kentik). 16.2% of IPv4 and 20.9% of IPv6 RPKI-covered routes have such 'open windows', ~18M more-specific prefixes forgeable today. RFC 9319 recommends leaving maxLength unset.

IPv6 RPKI (56%→79%) overtook IPv4 (54%→68%), reversing Job Snijders' 2024 'stalling' observation; addresses per ROA rose 2.31→2.62 and publication points 73→91. ~60% of unprotected US IPv4 is DoD space announced since 2021 for monitoring, not services.

Coverage can silently vanish: Mauritius fell 94%→69% after SEACOM (AS37100) lost four ROAs including a ~1M-address /12; Saudi Telecom and Orange Maroc saw ROAs disappear and return. A measurement trap: per-object checks that follow stale manifest links report hard failures on records that still produce valid routes via trust-anchor walk.

ASPA (path validation) grew 25x, 131 to 3,272 networks, driven by registry tooling. 9.7% of observed routing is ASPA-valid, but excluding trivially-passing short paths the published records verify ~3.5% (up from ~0.1%). Mid-path invalidity rose from ~0 to 0.048%; roughly a quarter of all mid-path failures trace to Syrian Telecom (AS29386) listing carriers that handle only 16% of its transit.
summary: IPinfo reports that RPKI-valid routed prefixes rose from 54.0% to 70.3% globally in a year (65.0% weighted by addresses), with China's jump from 3.7% to 83.0% supplying nearly 60% of the address-weighted gain. The analysis argues RPKI is now actually filtering bad routes rather than merely being adopted: valid and unknown prefixes reach a median ~595-596 collector peers while invalids reach a median of 2, and it shows raw country-level invalid-route percentages overstate harm (Spain's 28.2% falls to 0.057% once weighted by vantage-point visibility). It flags limits: RPKI validates origin only, not path, so attacks staying within a published ROA succeed, as in the August 2026 Hetzner AS24940 spoof that passed validation thanks to an over-broad maxLength and was used to obtain a TLS cert and push a malicious Virtualizor update; 16.2% of IPv4 covered routes have such open windows. It documents silent coverage loss (Mauritius 94%→69% after SEACOM dropped ROAs) and a measurement trap where per-object validators report false hard failures. ASPA path validation grew 25x to 3,272 networks but still checks only ~3.5% of routing beyond trivially short paths, and about a quarter of its mid-path failures trace to one operator, Syrian Telecom. All figures are self-reported from IPinfo's daily single-snapshot datasets built on RIPE RIS and RouteViews.
novelty: vantage-point-weighted analysis shows RPKI is actually filtering hijacks, not just adoption stats
audience: network/infrastructure security engineers, BGP operators

title: Superoptimizing an FPU emulator
why: An exhaustive instruction-sequence search found a branchless bit-twiddling formula a human could not, removing a mispredictable branch from a hot float routine, and it did so without a theorem prover or an LLM.
notes: The target routine extracts the lowest set bit of a float; the obvious bit-twiddling version breaks on powers of two, forcing an if branch the author wanted gone to avoid misprediction and slowing the common case.

The search enumerates loop-free formulas inductively by operation count, builds n-op expressions from pairs of smaller ones (a_ops + b_ops = n-1) across a fixed OPS set, and deduplicates identical value-vectors to prune the space.

Correctness is checked by evaluating candidates against a hand-picked set of representative bit patterns rather than a theorem prover; any counterexample found later is added to the test set and the search re-run.

The winning formula rewrites x & MANTISSA_MASK as x - (x & MANTISSA_MASK) and folds the negation into the subexpression a - x.to_bits() (equal to -(x & MANTISSA_MASK)), reusing a precomputed value to save one operation.
Caveat: the discovered formula flips the sign bit on powers of two, which the author deems acceptable for the use case; correctness rests on test coverage, not proof.
Code is destined for the author's work-in-progress FPU emulator; shared cost figures (op count, memory) are only partially quoted in the excerpt.
summary: The author needed a branchless way to extract the lowest set bit of a float, since the straightforward bit-twiddling version breaks on powers of two and required an if branch. Instead of hand-deriving a formula or using an LLM, they built a brute-force superoptimizer that inductively enumerates loop-free instruction sequences by operation count, deduplicating equivalent expressions as it grows them. Candidates are validated against a set of representative bit patterns rather than a theorem prover, with any counterexample fed back into the test set and the search repeated. The search found a branchless formula that saves one operation by rewriting x & MANTISSA_MASK as x - (x & MANTISSA_MASK) and merging the negation into the subexpression a - x.to_bits(), reusing an already-computed value. The result flips the sign bit on powers of two, which the author considers acceptable, and the code is intended for their work-in-progress FPU emulator.
novelty: brute-force superoptimizer discovers non-obvious bit-twiddling formula for FPU lowest-bit extraction
audience: low-level systems programmers and FPU/compiler implementers

title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
why: Before spending thousands of GPU-hours on the latest self-distillation RL method, this study finds none of ten contenders reliably beats plain GRPO on agent tasks.
notes: Ten representative self-distillation methods were compared head-to-head against a GRPO baseline on four agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Search-QA, WebShop) across three model sizes.
Scale of the study: 132 training runs, 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours, with repeated evaluation over eight rollout seeds for both pretrained backbones and all eleven trained methods.
Finding 1: gains over GRPO are limited in scope, with no method consistently winning across settings.
Finding 2: strong final task scores can hide unstable training dynamics.
Finding 3: more training compute does not reliably buy better performance.

The authors frame the motivation as a methodological critique: prior evaluations reuse published baseline scores under differing conditions, rarely compare contemporaneous methods directly, and underreport stability and cost. Scope is self-distillation agentic RL on these four benchmarks; results are not claimed to generalize beyond them.
summary: This paper is a controlled benchmark of self-distillation methods in agentic reinforcement learning, motivated by the observation that existing evaluations reuse published baseline scores under inconsistent conditions, rarely compare current methods directly, and neglect training stability and compute cost. The authors run ten representative methods plus a GRPO baseline on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop across three model sizes, totaling 132 training runs and 12,124.4 recorded H800 GPU-hours, with evaluation repeated over eight rollout seeds. They report three findings: gains over GRPO are limited with no method consistently ahead, strong final performance can mask unstable training, and additional training cost does not consistently yield better results. The work is positioned as a shared basis for fair comparison to steer future research toward reliable and cost-effective agent training. Results are confined to the tested self-distillation methods and benchmarks; the paper does not claim broader generalization.
novelty: rigorous benchmark showing self-distillation RL methods rarely beat plain GRPO
audience: ML researchers/engineers training agentic RL systems

title: Training the Whole Agent, Not Just the Model
why: If you train coding agents with RL against a fixed scaffold, you leave points on the table: co-evolving the harness added up to 12.6 pass@1 points over GRPO with a 9B model, and freezing tools at deployment costs up to 7.7.
notes: HarnessAdapt-RL updates the policy and the harness together during RL: a frozen teacher emits task-specific mechanism-level skills to fix flawed repair strategies, while a separate teacher evolves tools and hooks to address interaction problems recurring across tasks.
Each harness edit is accepted only if it raises the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either, so changes are gated on measured effect rather than heuristics.

Self-reported gains with a 9B base model: pass@1 over GRPO up 9.8 points on SWE-bench Verified, 12.6 on Multilingual, and 6.4 on Pro; the method also beats GRPO using the human-designed OpenHands harness.

Mechanism-level skill gains persist after the skills are removed at evaluation, suggesting the policy internalizes them; evolved tools and hooks are the opposite, and removing them at deployment costs up to 7.7 points.

Re-evolving tools and hooks as the policy changes beat freezing early harness versions; the trained artifact is a model-harness pair (policy plus evolved tools/hooks), with skills dropped at deployment.
Numbers are author-reported from the abstract; no training cost, teacher model identities, methodology detail, or baselines beyond GRPO and OpenHands are given in the provided text.
summary: The paper introduces HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains a coding-agent policy while simultaneously adapting the agent's harness during reinforcement learning, rather than keeping the harness fixed. A frozen teacher generates task-specific mechanism-level skills to correct flawed repair strategies, and a separate teacher evolves tools and hooks to fix recurring interaction problems, accepting a change only if it improves the observed pass rate or trainable rate without lowering either. New trajectories from the updated policy then guide further harness adaptation. With a 9B base model, the authors report pass@1 improvements over GRPO of 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, and claim it beats GRPO using the human-designed OpenHands harness. Skill gains persist after removal at evaluation, but removing evolved tools and hooks at deployment costs up to 7.7 points, so the trained output is a model-harness pair: the policy plus evolved tools and hooks, with skills removed at deployment. All figures are author-reported from the abstract, with no cost or detailed methodology in the provided text.
novelty: co-evolves agent harness (tools/hooks) alongside RL policy training
audience: researchers/engineers building coding agents and RL training pipelines

title: Matthew Garrett: Epic's EAC2 v2 seems fairly easily bypassable
why: Epic's EAC2 anti-cheat stack ties your ability to play to secure boot plus TPM attestation, and Garrett shows a ~$20 part defeats it, so the kernel-level requirement buys game security almost nothing on consumer hardware.
notes: EAC2 v2 (Linux) chains three things: an eBPF security-module monitor, required secure boot plus measured boot to prove a trusted kernel, and TPM remote attestation where the TPM signs boot measurements that a server verifies came from a real, vendor-certified TPM (via the Endorsement Key and vendor-signed EK certificate).

Attack 1: many desktop boards expose the TPM on a plugin module with a standard pinout including a reset pin; shorting it to ground briefly resets the TPM to its initial state, after which userland can write any measurements it wants and replay a known-good secure-boot log to produce a legitimately signed quote.

Attack 2 (for soldered/in-CPU/chipset TPMs): the quote only needs to come from *a* TPM, not the motherboard's. A Microchip USB-to-SPI bridge with a Linux driver lets you attach a cheap off-the-shelf TPM module, repoint /dev/tpmrm0 at it, and feed it trusted measurements. A modified kernel simply lies to the eBPF code about which TPM is in use.

Root cause Garrett names: remote attestation on PCs breaks wherever the verifier can't bind a specific TPM to a specific system, which is essentially all consumer machines (unlike managed enterprise fleets).

Caveat from the author: server-side detection could blocklist a flagged TPM, forcing a cheater to buy another, so the scheme may be practically good enough even though it is technically weak; whether $20-per-ban deters cheaters is left open.
summary: Matthew Garrett analyzes Epic's announced EAC2 v2 anti-cheat for Linux, which combines an eBPF-based security-module monitor with required secure boot, measured boot, and TPM remote attestation: the TPM signs boot measurements, and a server checks the quote came from a genuine vendor-certified TPM with the right secure-boot keys before admitting the player. He argues the measurement chain is trivially forgeable on consumer hardware. Discrete TPMs on standard plugin modules can be reset at runtime by shorting the reset pin to ground, letting userland write fabricated measurements and replay a legitimate secure-boot log to a modified kernel. Where the TPM is soldered or inside the CPU/chipset, a ~$20 Microchip USB-to-SPI bridge (with a Linux driver) lets an attacker attach an external TPM module, repoint /dev/tpmrm0 to it, and have a modified kernel lie to the eBPF code about which TPM is active. Garrett's underlying point is that PC remote attestation fails whenever the verifier cannot bind a specific TPM to a specific system, which holds for nearly all non-enterprise machines. He concedes the scheme may still be practically sufficient, since server-side detection can blocklist a compromised TPM and force cheaters to buy replacements, but he judges it technically weak.
novelty: TPM reset/swap defeats remote attestation anti-cheat
audience: security researchers and Linux kernel/anti-cheat engineers

title: Where Should a Stuck Agent Spend Its Next Tokens? Causal Attribution of Inference-Time Resources
why: If you build coding agents, the paper's central finding is that frontier models spend their extra inference budget on the resource that helps least: three of four pick test feedback 95-100% of the time yet repair fewer failures than if they had chosen at random.
notes: Banzhaf Resource Attribution (BRA) is a controlled factorial framework that measures each resource's marginal contribution to repair, plus interactions, while holding the failed state and revision protocol fixed; it separates three resource channels: computation, information, and feedback.
Evaluated on 194 function-level failures (MBPP+, HumanEval+) and 126 repository-level failures (SWE-bench Verified) across six models.
Ranked by measured repair value: task-relevant specifications consistently help; public-test feedback gives small gains; retrieved code gives little to none.
Value of extra computation declines as model capability rises, while information stays useful; channels mostly show diminishing returns, though complementary information can reinforce itself.
Three of four frontier models select feedback in 95-100% of cases and obtain lower repair gains than uniform random resource selection, exposing a gap between preferred and effective resources.
Claims are self-reported in the arXiv preprint; abstract gives no per-model repair numbers, model names, or significance tests for the random-selection comparison.
summary: The paper reframes inference-time scaling for failed coding agents as a choice among qualitatively different resources, computation, information, and feedback, rather than a single token-budget knob. It introduces Banzhaf Resource Attribution (BRA), a factorial framework that holds the failed state and revision protocol fixed and measures each resource's marginal contribution to repair and the interactions between them. Across six models on 194 function-level failures (MBPP+, HumanEval+) and 126 repository-level failures (SWE-bench Verified), task-relevant specifications consistently improve repair, public-test feedback yields small gains, and retrieved code adds little or nothing; the value of extra compute falls as model capability rises while information stays useful. Channels mostly show diminishing returns, but complementary information can reinforce itself. The headline result is a misallocation: three of four frontier models choose feedback 95-100% of the time yet repair less than uniform random resource selection would. The work is an arXiv preprint; the abstract omits model names, per-model numbers, and methodology for the random-selection baseline.
novelty: causal attribution shows agents misallocate inference-time resources on repair
audience: researchers and engineers building coding/agentic repair systems

title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
why: Enable persistent memory in a hosted LLM and a single poisoned entry can reinfect every fresh session, and on Claude it can spread across an organization and leak other users' prompts.
notes: The paper tests ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash, and claims all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across the three under one general threat model.

Memory-injection vectors span personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and MCP-connected resources; because state persists, attacks carry over into brand-new sessions rather than dying with the chat.
Demonstrated effects (self-reported): persistently spreading disinformation, generating harmful content, and simulating offline unresponsiveness, all triggerable in fresh sessions.
For Claude specifically, shared-memory features are said to let an attacker compromise multiple users within an organization and exfiltrate user prompts.

Authors derive defenses from their threat model and cybersecurity principles, and report that nearly half of the proposed mitigations are unimplemented across the evaluated services; datasets and attack artifacts are released.
Caveat: an arXiv abstract with vendor/model versions not publicly standard, no methodology, success rates, or dates in the text; all severity claims are the authors' and unverified here.
summary: This arXiv security paper examines "memory injection," a cross-session variant of prompt injection that exploits persistent memory in hosted LLM services to propagate malicious instructions beyond a single conversation. The authors present a general threat model and claim that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash.
